title: DEX Aggregators: Split Trades to Cut Slippage 💧
ig_caption:
Stop scrolling—this is how routers “water-fill” your swap 🚰

• You send 100 ETH → want USDC
• A DEX aggregator checks multiple pools (4 tanks)
• Instead of one big pour, it splits the order across pools
• Why? Each pool has different depth → different price impact
• The router aims for equalized price impact across the split
• Result: less slippage, smoother execution, better effective price
• If you don’t route (single-pool swap), your fill “sinks” into high impact

Practical takeaway: Slippage isn’t just a UI setting—it’s a measurable execution cost driven by pool depth. Route through aggregators and set sensible slippage limits to avoid surprise MEV and failed fills.

What’s your default swap style: split for best price, or single-route for simpler execution?
fb_caption:
DEX aggregators turn a single user swap into a routed execution across multiple liquidity pools—often described visually as “water-filling liquidity tanks.” In the reel: 100 ETH is swapped for USDC, but the router refuses to pour the whole amount into just one pool.

What’s happening on-chain
• On swap initiation, the aggregator queries multiple candidate routes/pools.
• Each pool’s available liquidity defines a curve (implicit order-book-like behavior). Large trades move along that curve, creating price impact.
• The router splits the order into fragments so that price impact is balanced (equalized) across pools.
• This reduces the marginal slippage per additional unit, improving realized output versus a single-pool fill.
• The “water-filling” model: fill shallower tanks first, then progressively use deeper liquidity so the “waterline” (effective execution price) doesn’t spike early.

Why splitting can help (and when it doesn’t)
• Lower slippage: splitting across deeper pools reduces execution cost.
• Better effective price: realized output increases relative to naive single-route routing.
• Trade-offs:
  – More legs/paths can increase routing complexity and execution risk.
  – Gas costs can rise with multi-hop or multi-pool routing.
  – MEV/ordering risk still exists: fragments get inserted into the mempool race environment.
  – Imperfect quotes: if pool states change between quote and execution, even “ideal” splits can deviate.

Security & execution implications
• Slippage limits matter: set a minimum acceptable output so adverse execution reverts.
• Beware stale quotes: always use aggregator-provided routing with tight tolerance.
• MEV awareness: large swaps are more likely to be targeted; splitting helps economics but doesn’t eliminate front-running/back-running.
• Smart contract trust: you’re relying on the router/aggregator’s execution logic and contract security.

Tokenomics angle (protocol-level)
• Many aggregators and DEX routers monetize via routing fees, affiliate incentives, or liquidity/provider incentives.
• For users, the “fee vs value” equation is key: the aggregator’s added execution overhead must be outweighed by reduced slippage.

Bottom line: Split routing is a deterministic response to liquidity depth and price impact curves. The best route is the one that maximizes realized output *after* fees and gas, while keeping slippage bounds tight enough to resist quote drift and MEV-induced variance.
threads_caption:
Routers don’t just “find a price”—they split your swap across multiple pools to equalize price impact (water-filling). If you swap in one pool, slippage spikes fast.

Would you rather optimize slippage or reduce execution complexity?
